solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Unravelling very fast (8)

blocks.note: a present participle: working out a code or a mystery
an informal British word for a brisk speed, as of a pace

annotation.surface: Something comes apart at speed.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses sit side by side with nothing between them; 'Unravelling very fast' reads as one phrase but splits after the first word.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: solving a code is cracking it, and British speech calls a very fast pace a cracking one.

entries.clue: Zany fellow dismissed by Nemo? (8)

indicatorNotes.dismissed: the fellow is sent away, so his letter drops out

blocks.note: Nemo, of the film Finding Nemo, is a clownfish
F = fellow; removed from CLOWNFISH

annotation.surface: A madcap character gets sacked by Captain Nemo.
annotation.walkthrough: Nemo suggests Jules Verne's captain, but the question mark points to the cartoon clownfish; take out F and CLOWNISH is left.
annotation.definitionFit: A zany person acts like a clown: clownish.

entries.clue: Wizards seek to recruit new blood (8)

indicatorNotes.to recruit: the wizards take on the new letter, bringing it inside their number

blocks.note: an ace or wizard is an expert
N = new; it goes inside ACES after the A
to seek to do something is to try

annotation.surface: A school of wizards hopes to sign up fresh talent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New blood' is a stock phrase for fresh recruits, so the eye reads it as one unit; 'new' is really N and 'blood' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Blood in the sense of lineage, as in 'of royal blood', is ancestry.

entries.clue: Ring sounding a little Dickensian (5)

indicatorNotes.sounding: what we need is the sound of the name, not its spelling

blocks.note: Little Nell is the heroine of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop

annotation.surface: A bell rings out with a faintly Victorian air.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A little Dickensian' looks like 'somewhat Dickensian'; it is Little Nell, and the silent K makes KNELL sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A knell is the ringing of a bell, especially for a death.

entries.clue: A man that line dances with no country music (8,6)

indicatorNotes.dances: the letters dance about into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
added to the fodder, making 14 letters

annotation.surface: A cowboy who line dances without any country and western playing.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sets up country and western line dancing; 'country music' is literally a nation's music.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal reading: the song a nation adopts as its own is, word for word, that country's music.

entries.clue: Start working without training (4)

indicatorNotes.without: in the old sense of outside: the working letters go round the training

blocks.note: a machine that is working is on
PE = physical education, school training

annotation.surface: Someone begins a job with no preparation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking; here it takes its old sense of outside, as in the hymn line 'a green hill far away, without a city wall'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, both verbs: a chairman begins a meeting by declaring it open.

entries.clue: On board, men catching rare sea creatures (6)

indicatorNotes.catching: the men catch the letter and hold it inside

blocks.note: pawns are the men on a chessboard
R = rare, as on a steak order

annotation.surface: The crew of a trawler haul in some unusual marine life.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a ship's crew; it is a chessboard, where pawns are called men.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: these small crustaceans are one kind of marine life among many.

entries.clue: Camper, perhaps, who can barely relax (6)

annotation.definition: Camper, perhaps, who can barely relax

blocks.note: not a tent-dweller but a guest at a particular kind of holiday camp, one where clothes are left off
reads as someone who hardly ever unwinds; really someone who can only unwind bare

annotation.surface: A tense holidaymaker who hardly ever unwinds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barely' reads as 'hardly'; it means unclothed, and 'camper' is someone at a nudist camp rather than a tent.
annotation.definitionFit: A nudist can only relax with no clothes on, and may well stay at a nudist camp.

entries.clue: Organ cleaner supported by wire (5,9)

indicatorNotes.supported by: in a down clue the first piece stands on top of the second

blocks.note: a daily is a cleaner who comes in each day, a British usage
a wire is a telegram, sent by telegraph

annotation.surface: Someone cleaning a church organ is propped up on a wire.
annotation.walkthrough: An organ here is a newspaper, the mouthpiece of a view; the Daily Telegraph is a British broadsheet.
annotation.definitionFit: A newspaper is an organ, a publication that voices opinion.

entries.clue: Dish composed of a metal (8)

indicatorNotes.composed: the letters are put together in a new arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A plate made out of metal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' does double duty: it reads as the link after 'composed', but its letters are part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Meatloaf is a baked dish of minced meat.

entries.clue: Short race arranged for pit workers (9)

indicatorNotes.arranged: the letters are set out in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A sprint is laid on for the miners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pit workers' suggests miners; the pit is the orchestra pit in front of a stage.
annotation.definitionFit: An orchestra plays in the pit of a theatre, so its members work there.

entries.clue: Mozambique’s back country bovid (5)

indicatorNotes.back: the back of the word is its final letter

blocks.note: the last letter of Mozambique
a land is a country

annotation.surface: An animal from the Mozambican backcountry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back country' reads as the outback; split it into the end of Mozambique and a word for country.
annotation.definitionFit: The eland is a large African antelope, a member of the cattle family, the bovids.

entries.clue: Some lotion, a salve for your nose (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters are used, a run lying inside the words

blocks.note: lotioN A SALve

annotation.surface: A dab of cream or ointment to soothe a sore nose.
annotation.walkthrough: The run starts with the last letter of 'lotion', steps over the comma, and ends inside 'salve'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain gloss of the adjective: from the Latin nasus, nose, as in a spray meant for your nose.

entries.clue: They sharpen colours on paintings (9)

indicatorNotes.on: one piece is placed on, after, the other

blocks.note: oils are oil paintings
tones are shades of colour

annotation.surface: Artists make colours brighter by laying them on their canvases.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sharpen colours' reads as one phrase; 'They sharpen' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Oilstones are whetstones, used with oil to sharpen blades.

entries.clue: Clear box housing old set of drawings (5,7)

indicatorNotes.housing: the box houses the letter, holding it inside

blocks.note: to strip a room is to clear it
a carton is a box
O = old; it goes inside CARTON

annotation.surface: A transparent case holds an old portfolio of sketches.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clear box' reads as a see-through case; 'Clear' is a verb here, giving STRIP.
annotation.definitionFit: A strip cartoon is a sequence of drawings telling a story, a comic strip.

entries.clue: They claim to forecast earnings for auditors (8)

indicatorNotes.for auditors: auditors are listeners, so the word is given as they hear it

blocks.note: profits are earnings

annotation.surface: Company forecasters predict profits for the accountants checking the books.
annotation.walkthrough: Auditors check accounts, which suits 'earnings'; the word's Latin sense is hearers.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: seers who say they can see what is coming, with 'claim to' allowing for doubt.

entries.clue: Harry, a short story writer’s city (8)

blocks.note: to harry someone is to nag them
as printed
Saki was the pen name of H. H. Munro, famed for short stories

annotation.surface: A man called Harry names a writer's home town.
annotation.walkthrough: Harry looks like a name; it is the verb to harass. The 's is 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the Japanese port on Kyushu is one city among many.

entries.clue: Way to goad fish (8)

blocks.note: ST = street, a way
to goad is to urge
on = to, as in 'turn the light to' or 'on'

annotation.surface: How to provoke a fish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To' giving ON is the unusual step: a door pushed to is closed, and the pieces run in answer order, not clue order, with 'to' last.
annotation.definitionFit: The sturgeon is a large fish, source of caviar.

entries.clue: Non-frozen spread for Pancake Day? (7,5)

blocks.note: frozen here means fixed in place; the opposite is movable
a spread is a lavish meal, a feast

annotation.surface: A butter that has not been in the fridge, for the pancakes.
annotation.walkthrough: Pancake Day is Shrove Tuesday, before Lent, and its date changes with Easter each year; the question mark marks it as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A movable feast is a church festival whose date varies, and Pancake Day is one.

entries.clue: Run, declining drinks, becoming parched (6)

indicatorNotes.drinks: declining takes the run in, as a drinker takes a drink

blocks.note: something declining is dying away
R = run, from cricket scoring; it goes inside DYING

annotation.surface: A runner, turning down any drinks, dries out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Declining drinks' reads as refusing a drink; 'drinks' is the verb that takes R in.
annotation.definitionFit: Drying means losing moisture, becoming parched.

entries.clue: A poet’s girl enlivened by sex (6)

indicatorNotes.enlivened: the girl is livened up, her letters jumbled

blocks.note: sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals
GIRL with its letters rearranged

annotation.surface: A poet's sweetheart is roused by physical passion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sex' looks like the obvious thing; it is the Latin number six, fitting for a Roman poet.
annotation.definitionFit: Virgil was the Roman poet who wrote the Aeneid.

entries.clue: Ironic, small label outside East Berlin landmark (9)

indicatorNotes.outside: the ironic word sits outside the East letter, holding it

blocks.note: 'that's rich' is said ironically
E = east; it goes inside RICH after the R
S = small, as in clothing sizes
a tag is a label

annotation.surface: A wry little sign put up outside a landmark in the old East Berlin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'East Berlin' is a ready-made phrase, but East is only E; the definition is 'Berlin landmark'.
annotation.definitionFit: The Reichstag is the German parliament building in Berlin.

entries.clue: Principal keeping one in step (5)

indicatorNotes.keeping: the principal keeps the one inside

blocks.note: the principal performer is the star
I = one, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: A head teacher keeps a pupil in line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In step' reads as a phrase meaning in time; 'step' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one tread in a staircase, the singular of 'stairs'.

entries.clue: Narrative cut short with maiden under attack (5)

indicatorNotes.cut short: the word loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.under: in a down clue M is placed below the first piece

blocks.note: a story, less its final Y
M = maiden, a maiden over in cricket

annotation.surface: A tale ends abruptly as a young woman is set upon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Under attack' is a stock phrase; 'under' places M and 'attack' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a verb: troops rush a castle's walls in a sudden assault.

entries.clue: After batting, turn first to the bar (5)

indicatorNotes.After: the turn comes after the batting
indicatorNotes.first: take the first letter of the word

blocks.note: a side that is batting in cricket is in
a go is a turn
the first letter of 'the'

annotation.surface: A cricketer, done at the crease, heads for the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To the bar' is the pub; T comes from 'first to the', and 'bar' is an ingot of gold.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: gold is cast into bars of a standard shape for storage in bank vaults.

entries.clue: Polish migrant able to speak at length (9)

indicatorNotes.migrant: the letters migrate, moving to new places

blocks.note: ABLE with its letters rearranged
to orate is to speak at length

annotation.surface: A migrant from Poland who can talk for ages.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Polish' with its capital suggests Poland; it is the verb, to refine.
annotation.definitionFit: To polish a piece of work is to elaborate it, refining its detail.

entries.clue: Sport of cane twirling (4)

indicatorNotes.twirling: the word is spun right round to face the other way

blocks.note: to cane is to flog

annotation.surface: A pastime of baton twirling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cane twirling' pictures a stick; cane is the verb to beat.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the club-and-ball game is one sport among many, and golfers do swing a stick.

entries.clue: York’s first-rate defender (8)

blocks.note: a regional word: how Yorkshire folk say 'excellent'
one who stands up for a person or a cause

annotation.surface: York has an excellent defender on its football team.
annotation.walkthrough: York stands for Yorkshire, where 'champion' is a northern English word of praise meaning excellent.
annotation.definitionFit: In Yorkshire something champion is first-rate, and a champion is one who defends a person or cause.
